text: Saying, Amen: Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and power, and might, be unto our God for ever and ever. Amen.
reflection: In John's vision, angels and elders fall before God's throne and worship: "Amen: Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and power, and might, be unto our God for ever and ever." Seven expressions of praise, a complete offering of worship. And notice that wisdom and thanksgiving appear side by side. The wisest response to God is gratitude. Those who see Him clearly, as these heavenly beings do, cannot help but give thanks. Gratitude is not merely good manners. It is the posture of a heart that understands reality. Everything we have comes from God. Every breath, every blessing, every grace is His gift. The wise life is a thankful life. As we begin this month focused on gratitude and contentment, join the worship of heaven. Before you ask God for anything today, thank Him. Name specific blessings. Let thanksgiving reshape your perspective. You will find that a grateful heart sees God's goodness everywhere.
question: Before you ask God for anything today, what specific blessings can you thank Him for?
prayer: Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honour, power, and might be unto You, our God, for ever. Give me a grateful heart that sees Your goodness everywhere. Amen.

text: Sing unto the LORD with thanksgiving; sing praise upon the harp unto our God…
reflection: The psalmist calls God's people to worship: "Sing unto the LORD with thanksgiving; sing praise upon the harp unto our God." Thanksgiving is meant to be sung. There is something about music that lifts our hearts and helps us remember God's goodness. The rest of the psalm gives reasons to sing. God heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. He counts the stars and calls them by name. He covers the heavens with clouds and provides rain for the earth. He feeds the animals and delights in those who hope in His mercy. From the vastness of the universe to the smallest creature, God is at work, and it is all cause for thanks. You do not need to be a skilled musician to sing to God. He delights in every grateful voice. Today, find a song of thanksgiving and sing it. In the car, in the kitchen, or quietly in your heart. Let music carry your gratitude to the God who cares for all.
question: What song of thanksgiving could you sing to God today?
prayer: Lord, You heal the brokenhearted and call the stars by name. I sing to You with thanksgiving, and I delight in praising You today. Amen.

text: By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name.
reflection: Hebrews describes a different kind of sacrifice: "By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name." In the Old Testament, worshippers brought animals and grain as sacrifices. Now, through Jesus, we bring praise. Our thankful words become an offering to God. The writer calls it the fruit of our lips. Just as a healthy tree naturally produces fruit, a heart rooted in Christ naturally produces thanksgiving. And notice the word continually. Not only when life is easy, but in every season. Sometimes praise is called a sacrifice because it costs us something. It is easy to praise God when everything is going well. But giving thanks in hardship is a true sacrifice. It declares that God is good even when we do not feel it. Today, offer the sacrifice of praise. Speak your thanks to God out loud, especially for something you are tempted to complain about.
question: What are you tempted to complain about that you could thank God for instead?
prayer: Lord, through Jesus I offer You the sacrifice of praise. Even when I do not feel it, I declare that You are good, and I give thanks to Your name. Amen.

text: Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God.
reflection: Paul explains why God blesses His people: "Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God." God enriches us so that we can be generous. And when we are generous, others give thanks to God. It is a beautiful cycle. God gives to us, we give to others, and their gratitude flows back to God. Our blessings are not meant to stop with us. They are meant to flow through us. When we hoard what we have, the cycle breaks. When we share it, thanksgiving multiplies. This also frees us from discontentment. When we see our resources as tools for blessing others rather than measures of our worth, we find joy in giving. We stop comparing and start sharing. Today, think about how God has enriched you, whether with money, time, skills, or relationships. Then find a way to share that blessing. Let your generosity cause someone else to give thanks to God.
question: How has God enriched you, and how could you share that blessing so others give thanks?
prayer: Lord, You enrich me so that I can be generous. Let Your blessings flow through me to others, so that their gratitude rises back to You. Amen.

text: And when he was come nigh, even now at the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen…
reflection: As Jesus rode toward Jerusalem, His disciples could not hold back: "the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen." They had witnessed healings, miracles, and lives transformed. Now they remembered it all, and their gratitude burst into loud praise. Remembering God's mighty works strengthens us. When we recall what He has done, our faith grows and our hearts are lifted. Gratitude is not only a feeling; it becomes fuel for the road ahead. The disciples did not know the suffering that awaited Jesus in Jerusalem that week. But their praise was right and good. And when some objected, Jesus said that if they were silent, the stones would cry out. Praise is that fitting. Today, remember the mighty works you have seen God do, in your life and in the lives of others. Let those memories turn into praise. Speak them aloud. Let gratitude strengthen you for whatever lies ahead.
question: Which of God's mighty works in your life could you remember and praise Him for today?
prayer: Lord, I remember the mighty works You have done in my life and in the lives of others. Let my memories turn into praise, and strengthen me for what lies ahead. Amen.

text: Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
reflection: Paul was addressing how the Corinthians worshipped together. Some prayed and gave thanks in tongues that no one else understood. So Paul asked, "how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?" Paul wanted thanksgiving to be shared. When we give thanks in a way others can understand, they can join in. They can say Amen. Gratitude becomes a community experience, not just a private feeling. This is a lovely reminder for our daily lives. Our thanksgiving can invite others to give thanks too. When we express gratitude clearly, at the dinner table, in conversations, or in a message to a friend, we help others notice God's goodness. Our thanks becomes contagious. Today, give thanks out loud in a way others can hear and understand. Share what you are grateful for. Invite someone else to say Amen with you.
question: What are you grateful for that you could share out loud so someone else can say Amen?
prayer: Lord, let my thanksgiving be shared and understood. Help me speak of Your goodness so others can join in and say Amen with me. Amen.

text: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
reflection: Proverbs 31 describes a woman of strength and character. And near the end comes this tender scene: "Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her." Her family recognizes her faithfulness and speaks words of honor. They do not take her for granted. They praise her openly. Wholehearted praise belongs first to God, but Scripture also encourages us to honor the people who bless our lives. Too often we assume people know we appreciate them. But words of praise are powerful. They encourage weary hearts and strengthen relationships. Think of someone in your life who works faithfully, often without recognition. A parent, a spouse, a friend, a coworker. When did you last tell them how much they mean to you? Today, rise up and call someone blessed. Speak specific words of appreciation. And give thanks to God, who places such faithful people in our lives.
question: Whom could you rise up and call blessed with specific words of appreciation today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the faithful people You have placed in my life. Help me honor them openly, and never take their love for granted. Amen.

text: Where is then the blessedness ye spake of? for I bear you record, that, if it had been possible, ye would have plucked out your own eyes, and have given them to me.
reflection: Paul reminds the Galatians of how they first welcomed him: "for I bear you record, that, if it had been possible, ye would have plucked out your own eyes, and have given them to me." When Paul arrived sick and weak, they received him with remarkable generosity. They would have given anything to help him. But now Paul asks, "Where is then the blessedness ye spake of?" Their joy had faded. False teachers had turned their hearts away from the gospel and from Paul. This is a gentle warning for all of us. The joy and generosity that mark the beginning of faith can fade if we drift from grace. Gratitude grows cold when we forget what we have received. But it can be rekindled. Today, remember the joy you felt when you first understood God's grace. Ask Him to restore that blessedness. And let renewed gratitude overflow into the kind of generosity the Galatians once showed.
question: Has the joy you felt when you first understood God's grace faded, and how could it be restored?
prayer: Lord, restore to me the joy I felt when I first knew Your grace. Renew my gratitude, and let it overflow in generosity toward others. Amen.

text: The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is blessed for evermore, knoweth that I lie not.
reflection: Paul had been listing his sufferings and weaknesses, and he wanted the Corinthians to know he was telling the truth. So he wrote, "The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is blessed for evermore, knoweth that I lie not." Even in the middle of defending himself, Paul paused to praise God. He described God as blessed for evermore, worthy of eternal praise. This shows us something about Paul's heart. Praise was not reserved for worship services. It came naturally, even in the middle of difficult conversations. His awareness of God was constant. And notice that praise and honesty go together. Paul spoke truthfully because he lived before a God who sees everything. Wholehearted praise shapes how we live. When we honor God continually, we become people of integrity. Today, let praise be woven into your ordinary moments. Bless God in the middle of tasks and conversations. And let your awareness of Him make you a person of truth.
question: How could you weave praise into the ordinary moments of your day?
prayer: God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, You are blessed for evermore. Let praise fill my ordinary moments, and make me a person of truth. Amen.

text: Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities.
reflection: Peter preached to a crowd in the temple and gave them wonderful news: "Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities." God sent Jesus to bless. That is His purpose. And the blessing He brings is not just material comfort. It is the deepest blessing of all: turning us away from sin and toward God. Sometimes we think of God's guidance as restrictive, a list of things we cannot do. But Peter shows that when God turns us from sin, it is a blessing. He is leading us away from what harms us and toward what gives life. Every time the Holy Spirit convicts us and redirects our steps, it is an act of love. Today, thank God for the ways He has turned you from destructive paths. And if He is nudging you to turn from something now, see it as a blessing. Follow His guidance. He sent Jesus to bless you.
question: Is God nudging you to turn from something, and can you see His guidance as a blessing?
prayer: Lord, You sent Jesus to bless me by turning me from my iniquities. Thank You for every destructive path You have turned me from. Help me follow Your guidance today. Amen.

text: Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.
reflection: Peter encourages believers to honor those in authority, describing governors as "them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well." Good government, at its best, restrains evil and honors what is good. Peter's point is that believers should be known for doing good, so that even those in authority will recognize it. Our lives should be so marked by goodness that praise naturally follows. But notice the deeper truth here. God designed the world so that good is worth honoring. Praise is the right response to goodness. That is why we praise God, the source of all goodness. And it is why we can honor the good we see in others. Today, practice noticing goodness. When someone does well, whether a coworker, a public servant, or a neighbor, tell them. And let your own life be marked by doing good. Most of all, give praise to God, from whom every good thing comes.
question: Whom could you praise today for doing well, whether a coworker, public servant, or neighbor?
prayer: Lord, every good thing comes from You. Help me notice and praise those who do well, and let my own life be marked by doing good. Amen.

text: Then again called they the man that was blind, and said unto him, Give God the praise: we know that this man is a sinner.
reflection: Jesus had healed a man born blind. But the religious leaders refused to accept it. They summoned the man and said, "Give God the praise: we know that this man is a sinner." They wanted him to thank God while denying that Jesus had anything to do with it. But the man would not be pressured. He simply said, "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." His honest testimony was the truest praise he could give. Giving God the praise means telling the truth about what He has done. It means giving credit where it is due, even when it is unpopular. The healed man was generous with the truth, and it cost him. He was thrown out of the synagogue. But Jesus found him and revealed Himself. Today, give God honest praise. Tell someone what He has done in your life, plainly and truthfully. Do not let pressure or fear silence your testimony. He deserves the credit.
question: What has God done in your life that you could tell someone about plainly and truthfully?
prayer: Lord Jesus, once I was blind, but now I see. Give me courage to give You honest praise and tell someone plainly what You have done for me. Amen.

text: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting: and let all the people say, Amen. Praise ye the LORD.
reflection: Book Four of the Psalms ends with a great doxology: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting: and let all the people say, Amen. Praise ye the LORD." From everlasting to everlasting. God's goodness has no beginning and no end. And the response is meant to be universal: let all the people say Amen. Not just the priests, not just the musicians, but everyone. Praise is a community invitation. This psalm had just recounted Israel's history of rebellion and God's patient mercy. Despite their failures, God remained faithful. So the people end with praise. That is often how gratitude works. When we look honestly at our own stories, we see how often we have failed and how faithfully God has carried us. That truth leads to worship. Today, look back over your life. See God's patient faithfulness through every season. Then join the chorus of all His people. Say Amen. Praise the LORD from everlasting to everlasting.
question: Looking back over your life, where can you see God's patient faithfulness in every season?
prayer: Blessed be the Lord from everlasting to everlasting. Thank You for Your patient faithfulness through every season of my life. I join all Your people in saying Amen. Amen.

text: (For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth;)
reflection: Paul describes what life in the light looks like: "For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth." Goodness, righteousness, and truth. These are the marks of a life made right with God. Notice that they are called fruit. They are not produced by straining or performing. They grow naturally as the Spirit works in us. Just as a tree does not strain to produce fruit, a life connected to God bears good fruit over time. Paul had just reminded the Ephesians that they were once darkness, but now they are light in the Lord. Being made right with God changes everything. And it calls us to walk as children of light. Goodness shows in how we treat others. Righteousness shows in our integrity. Truth shows in our honesty. Today, ask the Spirit to grow His fruit in you. Look for one way to show goodness, act rightly, and speak truthfully. Let your life reflect the light of the One who made you new.
question: Where can you show goodness, act rightly, or speak truthfully today?
prayer: Holy Spirit, grow Your fruit in me: goodness, righteousness, and truth. Let my life reflect the light of the One who made me new. Amen.

text: Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.
reflection: Paul lists the privileges God gave to Israel, and he ends with the greatest of all: from them, "as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen." Jesus came into the world through a particular family and nation, as a real human being. Yet He is also God over all, blessed forever. Paul cannot mention Christ without breaking into praise. That is what happens when we truly see who Jesus is. He is fully human, born into history. And He is fully God, worthy of eternal praise. The One who walked dusty roads, ate with sinners, and wept at a friend's grave is the same One who reigns over all. This truth deserves our wholehearted worship. Today, take a moment to marvel at who Jesus is. Think about His humility and His majesty. Then say Amen with Paul. Praise Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever.
question: What about Jesus, His humility or His majesty, could you marvel at today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are fully human and God over all, blessed forever. I marvel at Your humility and Your majesty, and I give You my wholehearted praise. Amen.

text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
reflection: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus pronounces a blessing on a special kind of person: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Peacemakers are not simply people who avoid conflict. They actively work to bring peace where there is division. They build bridges, seek reconciliation, and help others find common ground. And Jesus says they shall be called children of God. Why? Because they resemble their Father. God is the great Peacemaker. Through Jesus, He made peace between Himself and us, and He breaks down walls between people. When we make peace, we show the family resemblance. Peacemaking also brings contentment. A heart at peace with God and others is free from the restlessness of resentment. Today, look for an opportunity to make peace. Perhaps between two friends, in your family, or in your own heart. Take one step toward reconciliation. You will reflect the heart of your heavenly Father.
question: Where could you take one step toward peace, between friends, in your family, or in your own heart?
prayer: Father, make me a peacemaker. Give me courage to build bridges and seek reconciliation, so that I reflect Your heart as Your child. Amen.

text: Blessed be the kingdom of our father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest.
reflection: As Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowd shouted with joy: "Blessed be the kingdom of our father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna originally meant save us, but it had become a shout of praise. The people were celebrating the arrival of God's promised kingdom. They recognized that Jesus was the King they had been waiting for. Their praise was wholehearted. They spread cloaks and branches on the road. They shouted until the city stirred. Even though many did not fully understand what kind of King Jesus would be, their instinct to praise Him was right. He was worthy of every Hosanna. Today, join that ancient crowd. Lift your voice in praise to King Jesus. Celebrate His kingdom, which is still coming and will one day fill the earth. Let your Hosanna be both a cry for help and a shout of joy. He is the King who comes to save.
question: Where do you need to cry Hosanna, both as a plea for help and a shout of praise?
prayer: Hosanna, King Jesus! Save me where I need saving, and receive my praise. Blessed is Your kingdom that comes in the name of the Lord. Amen.

text: Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.
reflection: Proverbs speaks to married people with warm encouragement: "Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth." In the surrounding verses, a father warns his son against unfaithfulness and urges him to find joy in his own marriage. The image of a fountain suggests something refreshing and life-giving. God designed marriage to be a source of joy and delight, not something to take for granted. Contentment in marriage means choosing to rejoice in the person God has given you, rather than looking elsewhere. It means celebrating your spouse and cultivating the joy you share. Even if you are not married, this verse speaks to a broader truth. Contentment grows when we rejoice in the gifts God has already given us, instead of longing for what others have. Today, if you are married, find a way to bless and celebrate your spouse. And whatever your situation, thank God for the relationships He has given you. Rejoice in them.
question: How could you bless and celebrate someone close to you today instead of taking them for granted?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the relationships You have given me. Help me rejoice in them, celebrate the people I love, and be content with Your good gifts. Amen.

text: But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God.
reflection: Paul had been addressing a practical question about worship customs in Corinth. Then he closed the discussion with this: "But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." In other words, the churches of God are not built on arguing. A contentious spirit, one that loves to quarrel and win debates, has no place in God's family. When we remember God's goodness, contentiousness loses its grip. A heart full of gratitude does not need to fight over every point. It can hold convictions with grace. It can disagree without dividing. So much conflict in families and churches comes from forgetting what we have received. When we remember how patient God has been with us, we become more patient with others. Today, if you find yourself drawn into an argument, pause. Remember God's goodness to you. Ask whether this battle truly matters. Choose grace and unity over the need to be right.
question: When you are drawn into an argument, how can remembering God's goodness help you choose grace?
prayer: Lord, keep me from a contentious spirit. Fill my heart with gratitude for Your goodness, and help me choose grace and unity over the need to be right. Amen.

text: Rejoice over her, thou heaven, and ye holy apostles and prophets; for God hath avenged you on her.
reflection: In Revelation 18, John describes the fall of Babylon, a symbol of every proud, corrupt, and oppressive power that opposes God. Then comes a call to celebrate: "Rejoice over her, thou heaven, and ye holy apostles and prophets; for God hath avenged you on her." For centuries, God's people had suffered injustice. Now God has acted. Evil has been judged, and the oppressed have been vindicated. This rejoicing is not cruel delight in suffering. It is joy that justice has finally come. Wrong has been made right. God has kept His promise to defend His people. Many today still suffer under injustice. Some wait years for wrongs to be addressed. This verse assures us that God sees every injustice, and He will act. One day, all oppression will end. Today, if you are carrying the pain of injustice, take heart. God has not forgotten. Praise Him in advance for the justice He will bring. And pray for those still waiting.
question: What injustice are you carrying that you can trust God to set right?
prayer: Lord, You have not forgotten those who suffer injustice. I praise You in advance for the justice You will bring, and I pray for those still waiting. Amen.

text: (Howbeit there came other boats from Tiberias nigh unto the place where they did eat bread, after that the Lord had given thanks:)
reflection: John adds a small detail when describing where people searched for Jesus: it was "the place where they did eat bread, after that the Lord had given thanks." The miracle of feeding five thousand was remembered not just as the place of the bread, but as the place where the Lord gave thanks. That is striking. Before the bread multiplied, Jesus gave thanks for the little that was there: five loaves and two fish. Gratitude came first, and generosity followed. Jesus thanked the Father for a small offering, and God multiplied it to feed a multitude. There is a lesson here for us. We often wait until we have enough before we give thanks or give generously. But Jesus gave thanks for the little He had, and it became more than enough. Today, give thanks for what you have, even if it seems small. Offer it to God with gratitude. Let Him multiply it for His purposes. A grateful heart is ready to be generous.
question: What small thing could you give thanks for and offer to God to multiply?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You gave thanks for five loaves and two fish. I thank You for what I have, even when it seems small, and I offer it to You to multiply. Amen.

text: Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto thy holy name, and to triumph in thy praise.
reflection: The psalmist ends a long confession of Israel's failures with a prayer: "Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto thy holy name, and to triumph in thy praise." Notice the purpose of salvation in this prayer: to give thanks and to triumph in praise. God rescues His people not only for their good but so that they can worship Him. Thanksgiving is the goal of redemption. When we are saved, gathered, and restored, our response is gratitude. This reframes our prayers for help. When we ask God to rescue us, we can also offer Him our future praise. We can say: Lord, when You answer, I will give You thanks. And when He does, we must remember to follow through. Many people pray urgently in trouble but forget to give thanks when the answer comes. Today, think of a prayer God has answered. Have you thanked Him? Give Him that offering of gratitude now.
question: What prayer has God answered that you have not yet thanked Him for?
prayer: Lord, You save, gather, and restore Your people so that we can give You thanks. I thank You now for the prayers You have answered. Amen.

text: Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
reflection: Paul gives a simple instruction about how we talk: "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks." Notice the alternative he offers. Instead of crude talk, careless words, or mocking humor, he says to give thanks. Our words have power. They can tear down or build up. They can make light of what is sacred or honor what is good. Paul does not ban joy or humor. He is warning against speech that degrades people or treats serious things carelessly. And he offers a beautiful replacement: gratitude. When thankfulness fills our conversations, it changes the atmosphere. It lifts others up and points them toward God's goodness. Imagine if more of our conversations included thanks. At work, at home, online. Today, pay attention to your words. When you are tempted toward careless or unkind speech, replace it with thanksgiving. Speak about what you are grateful for. Let your words reflect a grateful heart.
question: How could you replace careless or unkind speech with thanksgiving today?
prayer: Lord, guard my words today. When I am tempted toward careless or unkind speech, fill my mouth with thanksgiving instead. Amen.

text: O LORD, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth.
reflection: Isaiah bursts into praise: "O LORD, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth." This is personal faith. Not just the LORD is God, but thou art my God. Isaiah had seen God's wonderful works, and he knew that God's plans, made long ago, were faithful and true. Living by faith means trusting God's long-term plans, even when we cannot see how everything fits together. His counsels of old, His purposes planned before time, are full of faithfulness. Nothing catches Him by surprise. Nothing derails His good intentions. When we remember the wonderful things God has done, our faith grows stronger for what we cannot yet see. Today, make this verse your own prayer. Tell God that He is your God. Praise Him for specific wonderful things He has done. And trust His faithful plans for your future. They are rooted in faithfulness and truth.
question: What wonderful things has God done that you can name as you praise Him today?
prayer: O Lord, You are my God. I will exalt You and praise Your name, for You have done wonderful things, and Your plans are faithful and true. Amen.

text: For it is written, Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not: for the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband.
reflection: Paul quotes a remarkable promise from Isaiah: "Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not: for the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband." In the ancient world, a woman without children often felt shame and sorrow. Yet God tells her to rejoice. He promises that she will have more children than anyone expected. Paul applies this to the people of God's promise. Through grace, the family of faith grows beyond what natural means could produce. This verse speaks comfort to anyone who feels barren or empty. Perhaps you are longing for something that has not come. Perhaps you feel unfruitful or overlooked. God can bring abundance from places of emptiness. He specializes in turning desolation into joy. This does not mean every longing will be fulfilled the way we expect. But it does mean that in God's presence, there is always hope. Today, rest in Him. Bring your empty places to Him and trust His abundance.
question: What empty place in your life can you bring to God, trusting His abundance?
prayer: Lord, You tell the barren to rejoice. I bring You my empty places and my unmet longings, and I trust that in Your presence there is always hope. Amen.

text: Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing.
reflection: Jesus told a parable about a servant left in charge of his master's household, giving food to the others at the proper time. Then He said, "Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing." The servant did not know when the master would return. But he was faithful in the ordinary tasks entrusted to him. And when the master came, he found him at work and blessed him. In Matthew, this parable comes in the middle of Jesus' teaching about His return. Its point is readiness. We do not know when Christ will come back, but we are called to be found faithful whenever He does. Readiness is not anxious watching of the sky. It is faithful doing of the work He has given. Feeding others, serving well, staying true. Today, be found so doing. Whatever task God has entrusted to you, do it faithfully. And look forward with joy to the blessing of the Master's return.
question: What ordinary task entrusted to you could you do faithfully today?
prayer: Lord, help me be found faithful in the ordinary tasks You have given me. Keep me serving well, and fill me with joy as I wait for Your return. Amen.

text: And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
reflection: Paul and Silas had been beaten and thrown into prison, their feet fastened in stocks. Yet Luke records something astonishing: "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." At midnight. In pain. In chains. They chose to praise. This is wholehearted praise at its most powerful. It does not depend on circumstances. It flows from a deep trust in God's goodness. And notice that the prisoners heard them. Their praise became a testimony. Others were listening. Shortly after, an earthquake opened the prison doors, and the jailer and his family came to faith. Our praise in hard places may reach people we do not even realize are listening. Today, if you are in a midnight season, try praising God anyway. Sing a song, speak a word of thanks, or pray with gratitude. Your praise may not change your circumstances immediately, but it will change your heart. And others may be listening.
question: What midnight are you in, and how could you choose to pray and sing praises anyway?
prayer: Lord, even at midnight and in chains, You are worthy of praise. Help me praise You in my hardest moments, and let others hear of Your goodness. Amen.

text: And as they did eat, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and brake it, and gave to them, and said, Take, eat: this is my body.
reflection: On the night before He died, Jesus shared a final meal with His disciples: "And as they did eat, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and brake it, and gave to them, and said, Take, eat: this is my body." Notice that He blessed before He broke. Jesus gave thanks to the Father for the bread that represented His own body, soon to be broken on the cross. Even facing suffering, He offered praise. This moment is at the heart of Christian worship. Through communion, believers remember His sacrifice with gratitude. The broken bread reminds us that He gave Himself completely. Our response is wholehearted praise. Jesus shows us that gratitude is possible even in the shadow of suffering. If He could bless God on the night of His betrayal, we can learn to give thanks in our hardest moments too. Today, remember the body of Christ given for you. Thank Him for His sacrifice. Let gratitude for the cross shape your whole life.
question: How can gratitude for the body of Christ given for you shape your day?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You blessed the bread and gave Your body for me. Thank You for Your sacrifice. Let gratitude for the cross shape my whole life. Amen.

text: For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him…
reflection: Melchisedec is one of the most mysterious figures in the Bible. He appears briefly in Genesis as "king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him." Abraham had just won a great battle. And in that moment of victory, a priest-king came to bless him and to bless God who had given the victory. Abraham responded by giving him a tenth of everything. Hebrews explains that Melchisedec points forward to Jesus, our eternal King and Priest. This scene teaches us how to respond to victory. When God gives us success, the right response is blessing and praise. Not boasting, not taking credit, but acknowledging God as the source. Abraham honored God with his gratitude and his gifts. Today, think of a recent victory or blessing. Pause to bless God for it. Give Him the credit. And remember that Jesus, our great High Priest, blesses us continually.
question: What recent victory or blessing could you pause to bless God for?
prayer: Lord Jesus, my great High Priest, You bless me continually. I give You the credit for every victory and blessing in my life, and I thank You. Amen.

text: Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing.
reflection: In Luke, Jesus tells a similar parable, but it comes right after Peter asks whether the teaching is for the disciples or for everyone. Jesus answers by describing a faithful steward set over the household to give everyone their portion of food at the right time. Then He says, "Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing." The emphasis here is on stewardship. Those entrusted with responsibility for others are called to care for them faithfully. Parents, leaders, teachers, mentors, anyone who has influence over others. Just a few verses earlier, Jesus gave a stunning promise: the master will serve those faithful servants himself. The Lord we serve is a Lord who serves. That truth should fill us with wholehearted praise. Today, think about the people entrusted to your care. Serve them faithfully, giving them what they need at the right time. And praise the Master who will one day bless and serve His faithful servants.
question: Who has been entrusted to your care, and how can you serve them faithfully today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the people You have entrusted to my care. Help me serve them faithfully, giving them what they need at the right time. Amen.

text: Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works…
reflection: Paul turns to David to explain how God makes people right with Himself: "Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works." Imputeth means to credit to someone's account. God credits righteousness to us, not because of our works, but as a gift received by faith. David knew this firsthand. After his great failures, he discovered the blessedness of being forgiven. In the next verses, Paul quotes him: blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven. This truth sparked the Reformation, remembered by many on this very day. Ordinary people rediscovered that salvation is by grace through faith, not by human effort. And it is still the most freeing message in the world. You do not have to earn God's approval. He credits righteousness to you through Christ. As this month of gratitude ends, give thanks for this greatest gift. Rest in the blessedness of being made right with God, without works, by His grace.
question: How does it feel to know that God credits righteousness to you without your works?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the blessedness of being forgiven and made right with You, not by my works but by Your grace. I rest in Your gift today. Amen.
